reason: The text describes the Israelites' oppression by Midian and their cry to God for deliverance (וַיִּזְעֲק֥וּ בְנֵֽי־ יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל אֶל־ יְהוָֽה), but this is a plea to God, not a complaint about their leaders. Gideon questions God about their suffering (וְלָ֥מָּה מְצָאַ֖תְנוּ כָּל־ זֹ֑את), but again, this is directed toward the divine, not against human leadership. The only interpersonal conflict described is when the men of the city demand that Joash bring out his son Gideon for destroying the Baal altar—but this is about religious practice, not complaints regarding leadership or governance.
